entities.name: Hartmann of Dillingen
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hartmann, Count of Dillingen, served as Prince-Bishop of Augsburg from 1248 until his death on July 11, 1286, a critical period during the late Staufer era and the tumultuous Interregnum of the Holy Roman Empire. As a scion of the powerful Swabian noble house of Dillingen, his episcopacy was defined by a steadfast allegiance to the Papacy, active participation in imperial politics, and a determined effort to consolidate the territorial integrity and administrative efficiency of his diocese amidst profound political fragmentation. His actions significantly influenced the ecclesiastical and political landscape of Swabia and Bavaria, shaping the future trajectory of the Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg as a key regional power.

Throughout his 38-year tenure, Bishop Hartmann navigated the complex power struggles between Emperor Frederick II and the successive popes, aligning consistently with the Roman See. Following Frederick II's death in 1250, he became a crucial player in the Interregnum, notably participating in the election of Rudolf I of Germany as King of the Romans in 1273, thereby helping to establish the Habsburg dynasty's initial imperial foothold. Domestically, he engaged in prolonged conflicts with the burgeoning imperial city of Augsburg over jurisdictional rights and urban autonomy, fiercely defending the temporal authority of his bishopric. He also undertook significant administrative reforms, including the reorganization of diocesan finances and the promotion of monastic life, strengthening the internal structure of the Prince-Bishopric.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hartmann of Dillingen was a highly significant regional figure, stabilizing the Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg during the tumultuous Interregnum and contributing to the rise of the Habsburg dynasty. His actions ensured the continued influence of his see for centuries.
